metadata.description: Name of the Log Analytics workspace that has Microsoft Sentinel enabled.

properties.displayName: AWS IAM user's access key used from a new IP
properties.query:
let History = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where UserIdentityType == "IAMUser";
let KnownPairs = History | distinct UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress;
let KnownUsers = History | distinct UserIdentityArn;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where UserIdentityType == "IAMUser" and SourceIpAddress !endswith "amazonaws.com"
| join kind=leftanti KnownPairs on UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress
| join kind=inner KnownUsers on UserIdentityArn
| summarize Calls = count(), Errors = countif(isnotempty(ErrorCode)), EventNames = make_set(EventName, 20), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress
| order by Errors desc, Calls desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Long-lived IAM access keys leak through code repositories, CI logs and laptops. When a key that normally runs from a
fixed set of IPs (a CI runner, an office) shows up somewhere new, it may be in someone else's hands. Only users with
at least one prior call in 30 days are included, so new users don't flood the results.
How to hunt: rank by Errors (stolen keys tend to hit AccessDenied while the attacker explores) and by unusual user
agents. Rotate any key you can't explain and move workloads to roles.

properties.displayName: AWS resources created in a region the account doesn't normally use
properties.query:
let Known = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | distinct RecipientAccountId, AWSRegion;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isempty(ErrorCode) and EventName matches regex @"^(Run|Create|Put|Start|Request|Import)"
| join kind=leftanti Known on RecipientAccountId, AWSRegion
| summarize Events = count(), EventNames = make_set(EventName, 20), Principals = make_set(UserIdentityArn, 10),
    IPs = make_set(SourceIpAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by RecipientAccountId, AWSRegion
| order by Events desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Attackers spin up instances, functions or clusters in regions the victim never looks at (cryptomining is the common
case, but also staging for exfiltration). This hunt lists accounts with create, run or put calls today in a region
that had no activity at all in the previous 30 days.
How to hunt: check the principals and event names. RunInstances or RequestSpotInstances with large instance types in
an unused region is almost always malicious. Disable unused regions with an SCP afterwards.

properties.displayName: Blocked by Conditional Access, then signed in elsewhere with a password only
properties.query:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend SingleFactorSuccess = ResultType == "0" and AuthenticationRequirement =~ "singleFactorAuthentication",
    CABlocked = ConditionalAccessStatus =~ "failure"
| summarize CAFailures = countif(CABlocked), FirstBlock = minif(TimeGenerated, CABlocked), BlockedApps = make_set_if(AppDisplayName, CABlocked, 10),
    SingleFactorSuccesses = countif(SingleFactorSuccess), LastSingleFactor = maxif(TimeGenerated, SingleFactorSuccess),
    SingleFactorApps = make_set_if(AppDisplayName, SingleFactorSuccess, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
    by UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| where CAFailures > 0 and SingleFactorSuccesses > 0 and LastSingleFactor > FirstBlock
| order by CAFailures desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Attackers holding a valid password often get blocked by Conditional Access on the first app they try, then probe
other apps, clients or protocols until one isn't covered. This hunt lists users with a CA failure followed later the
same day by a single-factor success.
How to hunt: compare the blocked apps with the successful ones. A success on an app or client your policies were
meant to cover is a policy gap to fix; a success from the same unfamiliar IP as the block is a compromised password.

properties.displayName: Users clicked links in mail from a sender domain never seen before
properties.query:
let KnownDomains = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where EmailDirection =~ "Inbound"
    | distinct SenderFromDomain;
let NewDomainMail = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where EmailDirection =~ "Inbound" and DeliveryAction =~ "Delivered"
    | where SenderFromDomain !in (KnownDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress = tolower(RecipientEmailAddress), SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, Subject;
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActionType =~ "ClickAllowed" or IsClickedThrough == true
| extend AccountUpn = tolower(AccountUpn)
| join kind=inner NewDomainMail on NetworkMessageId, $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| summarize ClickerCount = dcount(AccountUpn), Clickers = make_set(AccountUpn, 20), Urls = make_set(Url, 10), FirstClick = min(TimeGenerated)
    by SenderFromDomain, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by ClickerCount desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Phishing often comes from freshly registered or lookalike domains that Defender hasn't classified yet. This hunt
lists sender domains that first mailed the organization in the last day and whose links were clicked, ranked by how
many people clicked.
How to hunt: look for lookalikes of your own domain or of suppliers, and for domains registered in the last few
weeks. If a domain is malicious, check the clickers' sign-ins (AiTM, MFA registration) right after the click.

properties.query:
let dormancy = 30d;
let Recent = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) and ResultType == "0"
    | summarize ReturnedAt = min(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Location, 10) by UserPrincipalName;
let Previous = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(1d)) and ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSeenBefore = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName;
Recent
| join kind=inner Previous on UserPrincipalName
| where ReturnedAt - LastSeenBefore > dormancy
| extend DaysDormant = datetime_diff("day", ReturnedAt, LastSeenBefore)
| project UserPrincipalName, DaysDormant, LastSeenBefore, ReturnedAt, IPs, Countries
| order by DaysDormant desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Accounts that haven't been used for a month or more are favorite targets: nobody notices when they come back to life.
This lists successful sign-ins in the last day by accounts whose previous successful sign-in was more than 30 days ago.
How to hunt: check each against HR records (leave, departures) and the account owner. Former employees and service
accounts are the high-priority cases.

properties.displayName: First use of Azure or Graph command-line tools by a user
properties.query:
let AdminApps = dynamic(["Microsoft Azure PowerShell", "Microsoft Azure CLI", "Graph Explorer", "Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools",
    "Azure Active Directory PowerShell", "Microsoft Exchange REST API Based Powershell", "Microsoft Intune PowerShell"]);
let Known = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where AppDisplayName in (AdminApps)
    | distinct UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName), AppDisplayName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0" and AppDisplayName in (AdminApps)
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| join kind=leftanti Known on UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), SignIns = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Locations = make_set(Location, 5)
    by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| order by FirstSeen desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Azure PowerShell, Azure CLI, Graph Explorer and the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK are how attackers (and tools like
GraphRunner and ROADtools that impersonate them) query and change a tenant after taking over an account. This hunt
lists users who signed in to one of these apps today and hadn't in the previous 30 days.
How to hunt: expect admins and developers; focus on users outside IT, sign-ins from unfamiliar IPs, and users who
also show up in the Graph enumeration rule or the device code rule.

properties.displayName: One account logging on to many devices over the network
properties.query:
DeviceLogonEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess" and LogonType in ("Network", "RemoteInteractive")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceName), Devices = make_set(DeviceName, 50), SourceIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountDomain, AccountName
| where DeviceCount >= 10
| order by DeviceCount desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Lateral movement looks like one account (often a stolen admin or service account) making network or RDP logons to
many machines in a short time. This hunt lists user accounts with successful network or remote-interactive logons to
ten or more devices in the last day.
How to hunt: management servers, vulnerability scanners and backup accounts will top the list; note them once. Focus
on regular user accounts, accounts that don't normally do this, and source IPs that are workstations.

properties.displayName: Large numbers of mail items deleted from a mailbox
properties.query:
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange" and Operation in ("HardDelete", "SoftDelete", "MoveToDeletedItems")
| summarize HardDeletes = countif(Operation == "HardDelete"), SoftDeletes = countif(Operation == "SoftDelete"),
    MovedToDeleted = countif(Operation == "MoveToDeletedItems"), ClientIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Actor = UserId, MailboxOwnerUPN
| where HardDeletes >= 50 or (HardDeletes + SoftDeletes + MovedToDeleted) >= 500
| extend ActorIsOwner = tolower(Actor) == tolower(MailboxOwnerUPN)
| order by HardDeletes desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Bulk deletion of mail can be an attacker covering tracks (deleting sent phishing, security notifications or replies
from a fraud victim), an insider destroying records, or someone tidying their inbox. Hard deletes (bypassing Deleted
Items) are the more interesting signal.
How to hunt: look at rows where the actor isn't the mailbox owner, or where the client IP is unfamiliar. Pair with
the inbox-rule rules and with sign-ins for the same user around the same time.

properties.query:
let minDenials = 5;
let Window = SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d);
Window
| where ResultType == "500121"
| summarize Denials = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstDenial = min(TimeGenerated), LastDenial = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserPrincipalName, Hour = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Denials >= minDenials
| join kind=leftouter (
    Window | where ResultType == "0" | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName
  ) on UserPrincipalName
| extend SuccessAfterDenials = isnotnull(LastSuccess) and LastSuccess > FirstDenial
| project UserPrincipalName, Hour, Denials, FirstDenial, LastDenial, SuccessAfterDenials, LastSuccess, IPs
| order by SuccessAfterDenials desc, Denials desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
MFA fatigue attacks bombard a user with push prompts until they approve one. Look for users with a burst of denied or
failed MFA prompts in an hour, then check whether a successful sign-in followed.
How to hunt: start with rows where SuccessAfterDenials is true. Call the user (not by email) and ask whether they
approved a prompt they didn't start. If so, revoke sessions and reset credentials.

properties.displayName: Regular-interval connections to a public IP (C2 beaconing)
properties.query:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess" and isnotempty(RemoteIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| sort by DeviceName asc, InitiatingProcessFileName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, TimeGenerated asc
| extend SameFlow = DeviceName == prev(DeviceName) and InitiatingProcessFileName == prev(InitiatingProcessFileName)
    and RemoteIP == prev(RemoteIP) and RemotePort == prev(RemotePort)
| extend Gap = iff(SameFlow, datetime_diff("second", TimeGenerated, prev(TimeGenerated)), long(null))
| where isnotnull(Gap)
| summarize Connections = count() + 1, AvgGapSeconds = avg(Gap), StdevGap = stdev(Gap), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), RemoteUrl = take_any(RemoteUrl)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where Connections >= 50 and AvgGapSeconds >= 10
| extend Jitter = round(StdevGap / AvgGapSeconds, 3)
| where Jitter < 0.2
| order by Jitter asc, Connections desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Command-and-control implants check in on a timer (every 60 seconds plus a little jitter, for example). This hunt
finds process-to-destination pairs with 50+ connections in a day whose gaps between connections barely vary
(Jitter = standard deviation / mean of the interval, below 0.2).
How to hunt: start with the lowest Jitter and the least-known processes. Update agents, telemetry and NTP will show
up with near-zero jitter too; check the destination (RemoteUrl, WHOIS, threat intel) and the process path before
digging into the device.

properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName == "Consent to application" and Result =~ "success"
| mv-apply Prop = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties on (
    where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "ConsentAction.Permissions"
    | extend Permissions = tostring(Prop.newValue)
  )
| extend MailScopes = extract_all(@"((?:Mail|MailboxSettings|EWS)\.[\w\.]+|full_access_as_app)", Permissions)
| where array_length(MailScopes) > 0
| summarize Consents = count(), ConsentedBy = make_set(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), 25),
    Scopes = make_set(MailScopes), LastConsent = max(TimeGenerated)
    by AppName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), AppId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id)
| order by LastConsent desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Lists every app that received mail permissions through consent in the last 30 days, with who consented. Mail access is
what business email compromise needs, and apps keep that access after a password reset.
How to hunt: review each app's publisher and purpose; revoke anything unknown in Entra ID (Enterprise applications),
and check the consenting users' recent sign-ins.

properties.displayName: Rare executables run from user-writable folders
properties.query:
let Prevalence = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where isnotempty(SHA256)
    | summarize DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceName) by SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(SHA256)
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\(appdata|temp|downloads|users\\public|programdata|perflogs)\\"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Executions = count(), Devices = make_set(DeviceName, 5), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 5),
    Parents = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5) by SHA256, FileName
| join kind=inner Prevalence on SHA256
| where DeviceCount <= 2
| project FirstSeen, FileName, SHA256, DeviceCount, Executions, Devices, Paths, Parents
| order by DeviceCount asc, FirstSeen desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Malware usually runs from Downloads, AppData, Temp, Public or ProgramData, and a new payload's hash is seen on only one
or two devices. This hunt lists binaries run from those folders in the last day whose SHA256 appears on two or fewer
devices across the whole estate in the last week.
How to hunt: look the hashes up (Defender file page, VirusTotal), check the signer and the parent process. Anything
unsigned launched by an Office app, a browser or a script host comes first.

properties.displayName: Successful sign-ins with rarely seen user agents
properties.query:
let maxSeen = 3;
let AgentCounts = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) and ResultType == "0"
    | summarize TimesSeen = count(), UsersWithAgent = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by UserAgent;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) and ResultType == "0"
| join kind=inner (AgentCounts | where TimesSeen <= maxSeen) on UserAgent
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserAgent, TimesSeen, UsersWithAgent, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName
| order by TimesSeen asc, TimeGenerated desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Attack tools and scripts (python-requests, curl, unusual browsers) often show up as user agents almost never seen in
your tenant. Lists successful sign-ins in the last day whose user agent appeared three or fewer times in 30 days.
How to hunt: script-like agents on interactive user accounts are the top priority; then agents tied to a single user
from a new IP.

properties.displayName: New credentials added to an app or service principal
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName == "Add service principal credentials" or OperationName has "Certificates and secrets management"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), AppId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, AppName, AppId, Actor, ActorIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
Adding a secret or certificate to an existing app lets an attacker authenticate as that app, often with broad API
permissions and no MFA. Legitimate rotations happen, so this is a hunt, not an alert.
How to hunt: focus on apps with high-privilege permissions, credentials added by people who don't own the app, and
changes outside your normal rotation schedule.

properties.displayName: Bulk download from a SharePoint site the user hasn't used before
properties.query:
let Known = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint", "OneDrive")
    | distinct UserId, Site_Url;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint", "OneDrive") and Operation in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| join kind=leftanti Known on UserId, Site_Url
| summarize Files = dcount(SourceFileName), SampleFiles = make_set(SourceFileName, 10), ClientIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 5),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by UserId, Site_Url
| where Files >= 25
| order by Files desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
People mostly work in the same handful of sites. Downloading 25+ files from a site the user hasn't touched in 30 days
is how both departing employees and attackers with a stolen session collect data, and it stays under the tenant-wide
mass-download threshold.
How to hunt: check whether the site matches the user's job (HR files pulled by an engineer is the classic case), and
whether the downloads came from a managed device or an unfamiliar IP.

properties.displayName: Storage account keys listed by a new caller
properties.query:
let Known = AzureActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1d))
    | where OperationNameValue =~ "MICROSOFT.STORAGE/STORAGEACCOUNTS/LISTKEYS/ACTION"
    | distinct Caller;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OperationNameValue =~ "MICROSOFT.STORAGE/STORAGEACCOUNTS/LISTKEYS/ACTION" and ActivityStatusValue in~ ("Success", "Succeeded")
| where Caller !in (Known)
| summarize StorageAccountCount = dcount(_ResourceId), StorageAccounts = make_set(_ResourceId, 20), IPs = make_set(CallerIpAddress, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by Caller
| order by StorageAccountCount desc

tags.name: description
tags.value:
A storage account key gives full access to every blob, file share, queue and table in the account, and it isn't tied
to the caller's identity, so later data access doesn't show who did it. Listing keys is noisy (the portal does it),
so this is a hunt: callers who listed keys today and hadn't in the previous 14 days.
How to hunt: callers listing keys on many accounts at once rank first. Check whether the account then showed reads
from unfamiliar IPs (StorageBlobLogs, if collected), and consider disabling shared key access entirely.
